A.explanation: Point A is maximum positive displacement, so nearby particles are all displaced to the right and not crowded together.

B.explanation: Particles just left of B are displaced right and particles just right of B are displaced left, so they move toward each other to form a compression.

C.explanation: Point C is maximum negative displacement, so nearby particles are all displaced to the left and not crowded together.

D.explanation: Particles just left of D are displaced left and particles just right of D are displaced right, so they spread apart to form a rarefaction.

hints: Notice the axes show particle displacement against distance, with positive meaning displaced to the right and negative meaning displaced to the left.
Recall a compression needs particles on both sides to be displaced toward the same place, so focus on the zero-displacement crossings where the sign changes.
Compare the sign of displacement just left and just right of each zero crossing to see where particles converge and where they diverge.
walkthrough: The graph is displacement-distance for a longitudinal wave, so each $y$-value tells how far that particle is shifted right if positive or left if negative from its equilibrium position.
A compression is where neighbouring particles are pushed together, so particles to the left must be shifted right ($>0$) and particles to the right must be shifted left ($<0$).
At the peaks A and C the displacement is maximum, so neighbours on both sides are shifted the same way and there is no crowding.

At the zero crossings the displacement changes sign. On the falling crossing, displacement goes from positive on the left to negative on the right, so left particles move right and right particles move left toward the crossing.
On the rising crossing, displacement goes from negative on the left to positive on the right, so particles move away from the crossing, giving a rarefaction.
Therefore the falling zero-displacement point is the compression. This is option B.
